items.q: Why can looking confident still make you sound weak?
items.a: Status is judged through **visual image and vocal image**. The moment you open your mouth, vocal image can undo the suit, posture, and smile.

items.q: How should high-status speakers end their sentences?
items.a: End on a **lower pitch**. Rising **uptalk** can be a cooperative habit (e.g. Australia) but reads as insecurity elsewhere — and 10 years of reps make it invisible to you.

items.q: Why does saying more make you sound weaker?
items.a: High **message density** raises cognitive load — listeners excavate your point from too many words. **Fewer words = more weight per word.**

items.q: What is the PAT framework for on-the-spot answers?
items.a: **Pause → Ask a clarifying question → "The one thing."** Clarifying shrinks a vague question so you answer precisely instead of covering every interpretation.

items.q: How do you hold eye contact one-on-one without freaking out?
items.a: Use the **triangle technique**: left eye → right eye → nose bridge for extended contact without a staring contest.

items.q: How should you use eye contact in a group?
items.a: **One person, one thought, then move** (singular eye contact). Avoid darting, robotic scanning, A-B-C loops, looking over heads, or locking on one person.

items.q: How do high-status communicators activate imagination?
items.a: Use **specificity**, **analogies/metaphors/similes**, and storytelling instead of bullet-point facts. Storytelling is the ultimate influence weapon in the toolkit.

items.q: Why does embracing silence raise your status?
items.a: Pause builds weight, processing time, respect, deliberation, and space for others. Fillers (**um, ah, "you know"**) signal uncertainty even when content is strong.

items.q: What homework does the video assign for this week?
items.a: Apply **lower pitch endings** and **PAT** in your next conversation — traits 5 and 4 from the countdown.
